about: Earliest dated places of the newer place groups (bidb.oldest_checks, roadmap N5), each checked against its sources. verdict: kept (the date holds), corrected (year and age_text from the sources), dropped (reason: wrong kind of place, the date of something else, or no support). Sources carry exact quotes, checked by python -m bidb.evidence --check.

entries.name: St Mary's Chapel and graveyard
entries.reason: 1367 is when the chapel at Newhills (St Mary's of Stoneywood) was ordered to be completed; the graveyard belongs to it and was in use until the 20th century. Strictly a chapel graveyard rather than a cemetery.

sources.title: St Mary's Chapel and graveyard, Chapel Farm (SM10446)
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: was ordered to be completed in 1367 and was last mentioned in 1649, when the Kirk Session of St Machar's prohibited further burials within the churchyard

entries.name: Poets' Corner
entries.reason: Poets' Corner is the south transept of Westminster Abbey, a place of burials and memorials inside a church, not a cemetery; 1400 is Chaucer's burial.

sources.title: Poets' Corner
sources.quote: The first poet interred in Poets' Corner was Geoffrey Chaucer in 1400.

entries.name: St Swithin's Cemetery, Gillmoss
entries.reason: 1425 is the traditional date of the first Mass at the Gillmoss chapel (St Swithin's RC church), according to parish lore, not a date for the cemetery; no source dates the burial ground itself.

entries.name: Cross Bones
entries.reason: 1598 is the first known mention of the burial ground (Stow's Survey of London); it may be older, and closed in 1853.

sources.title: Cross Bones
sources.quote: The earliest known mention of the cemetery comes from John Stow's A Survey of London (1598)

entries.name: The Cabbage Garden, Dublin
entries.reason: The plot was granted to St Patrick's Cathedral as a cemetery in 1666 and used for burials until the 1890s.

sources.title: Cabbage Garden, Dublin
sources.quote: Used as a cemetery from 1666 until the 1890s, it is now laid-out as a public park.

entries.name: Height Quaker Burial Ground
entries.reason: The Friends' burial ground at Height (Upper Allithwaite) was first used about 1676, as its inscribed lintel and the Historic England list description of its walls state.

sources.title: Height Quaker burial ground (Old Cumbria Gazetteer)
sources.author: Martin and Jean Norgate
sources.locator: Listed Buildings 2010 entry for Friend's Burial Ground Walls
sources.quote: Entrance to south end has wide door in porch with gabled roof, the lintel inscribed: "FRIENDS BURIAL GROUND HEIGHT FIRST USED c.1676".

entries.name: Huguenot cemetery, Dublin
entries.reason: The Huguenot cemetery on Merrion Row dates from 1693; the last burial was in 1901.

sources.title: Huguenot Cemetery, Dublin
sources.quote: is a small cemetery dating from 1693 located near St

entries.name: East Sheen Cemetery
entries.reason: Wikidata's 1786 has no support; the cemetery was opened (as Barnes Cemetery) in 1905 or 1906 on former woodland.

sources.title: East Sheen Cemetery
sources.quote: The cemetery opened in 1906 on what was previously woodland in a rural area of Surrey.

entries.name: Kirkbean Church And Churchyard
entries.reason: 1776 is the date of the present church, which incorporates an earlier church, so the churchyard is at least that old; the record is the church with its churchyard.

sources.title: Kirkbean Parish Church and churchyard (LB10374)
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: Dated 1776. T-plan church incorporating existing church as east jam

entries.name: Grave of George Orwell
entries.reason: Orwell was buried in All Saints' churchyard, Sutton Courtenay, on 26 January 1950; the grave dates from then.

sources.title: George Orwell
sources.quote: David Astor arranged for Orwell to be interred in the churchyard of All Saints' Church, Sutton Courtenay, on 26 January 1950.

entries.name: Grave of Dylan Thomas
entries.reason: Dylan Thomas died in New York in November 1953 and was buried in St Martin's churchyard, Laugharne, later that month.

sources.title: Dylan Thomas
sources.quote: He died on 9 November, and his body was returned to Wales. On 25 November, he was interred at St. Martin's churchyard in Laugharne, Carmarthenshire.

entries.name: Howard Mausoleum
entries.reason: The pyramid mausoleum was commissioned in 1785 for Ralph Howard, 1st Viscount Wicklow.

sources.title: Howard Mausoleum
sources.quote: Howard Mausoleum was erected in County Wicklow, Ireland, commissioned in 1785, for the first Viscount of Wicklow, Ralph Howard.

entries.name: The Mausoleum of John Fuller in the Churchyard to the South East of the Church
entries.reason: Smirke's pyramid for 'Mad Jack' Fuller was erected in his lifetime in 1810.

sources.title: The Mausoleum of John Fuller in the Churchyard to the South East of the Church (list entry 1232442)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: He died on the 19th April 1833, but it was erected in his lifetime in 1810.

entries.name: The Raikes Mausoleum
entries.reason: Built for Sir Robert Raikes in 1818 (inscription MDCCCXVIII).

sources.title: The Raikes Mausoleum (list entry 1203947)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Mausoleum. 1818 for Sir Robert Raikes. Limestone ashlar. Circular plan: probably a copy of a Roman model.

entries.name: Unidentified Mausoleum
entries.reason: One of the earliest monuments in Kensal Green Cemetery, illustrated in 1834.

sources.title: Unidentified Mausoleum, Kensal Green Cemetery (list entry 1389248)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: One of the very earliest monuments in the cemetery, and one of a pair. Illustrated in The Penny Magazine, August 2nd 1834.

entries.name: O'Loghlen Mausoleum
entries.reason: No source found for 1855; local histories say Sir Michael O'Loghlen (d. 1842) lies in the uninscribed Egyptian-style family mausoleum at Ruan old graveyard, but give no building date.

entries.name: Trench Mausoleum
entries.reason: Wikidata holds two dates: 1858 (a tourism page) and c. 1790 (the National Inventory of Architectural Heritage, which dates it 1780-1800). The official inventory's c. 1790 is taken.

sources.title: Trench's Monument, Moneyveen, Galway (Reg. 30407317)
sources.author: National Inventory of Architectural Heritage
sources.quote: Freestanding round-plan three-stage tower set within round-plan enclosure having gravestones, built c.1790.

entries.name: Mausoleum Of Hartley Family In Highgate (Western) Cemetery
entries.reason: The Hartley family's Egyptian mausoleum in Highgate Cemetery is dated 1860, by Patrick MacDowell.

sources.title: Mausoleum of Hartley family in Highgate (Western) Cemetery (list entry 1378883)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Hartley family mausoleum. 1860. By P MacDowell, RA (active 1822-70). Massive Egyptian mausoleum of grey granite with battered sides

entries.name: Mausoleum of Emma Guerrier, Highgate Cemetery
entries.reason: The list entry dates the mausoleum only by Mrs Guerrier's death in 1872; it was presumably built then.

sources.title: Monument to Mrs Emma Guerrier in Highgate (Western) Cemetery (list entry 1378916)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Monument to Mrs Emma Guerrier, d.1872. Mausoleum. Pediments to each face, grey granite columns with inset corners, Portland stone side walls.

entries.name: Tomb of Mary Ellis in St Clement's Church
entries.reason: Chest tomb of Mary Ellis, who died in 1609; the plaque on its base is a modern (c. 1970) addition.

sources.title: Tomb of Mary Ellis, St Clement's Church, Leigh-on-Sea (list entry 1485951)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A chest tomb dedicated to Mary Ellis in 1609. MATERIALS The tomb comprises a limestone slab on a red brick base laid in English bond.

entries.name: Tomb of William Goodlad in St Clement's Church
entries.reason: Chest tomb of Captain William Goodlad, who died in January 1639.

sources.title: Tomb of William Goodlad, St Clement's Church, Leigh-on-Sea (list entry 1481914)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A chest tomb dedicated to William Goodlad in 1639. MATERIALS Limestone. PLAN Orientated on an east to west axis.

entries.name: Tomb of John Tradescant and his family
entries.reason: The Tradescant tomb at St Mary's, Lambeth, is a 1662 carved sarcophagus; its lid dates from the 1853 restoration.

sources.title: Tomb of John Tradescant and his family in St Mary's Churchyard (list entry 1116214)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: 1662 hard sandstone sarcophagus with high relief carvings on all four sides depicting classical and Egyptian ruins

entries.name: Tomb of Mary Anna Haddock in St Clement's Church
entries.reason: Chest tomb of Mary Anna Haddock (d. 1688), daughter of William Goodlad.

sources.title: Tomb of Mary Anna Haddock, St Clement's Church, Leigh-on-Sea (list entry 1481879)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A chest tomb dedicated to Mary Anna Haddock in 1688. MATERIALS Limestone. PLAN Orientated on an east to west axis.

entries.name: Table tomb to John Davies of Dunham, south east of Church of St Mary
entries.reason: The list entry dates the table tomb to 1726.

sources.title: Table tomb to John Davies of Dunham, Thornton-le-Moors (list entry 1145887)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Table tomb. 1726. John Davies of Dunham. Sandstone base has 2 sunk panels parts buried.

entries.name: Tombchest Of John Kitto, 6 Metres To South Porch Of Church Of St Ivo
entries.reason: Erected by John Kitto for his son, buried December 1749.

sources.title: Tombchest of John Kitto, St Ive (list entry 1137074)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Tombchest. Circa 1749. Erected by John Kitto in memory of John his son, buried December 1749 and Mary his daughter buried March 1737.

entries.name: Tombchest  Of William Rattle 6 1/2 Metres North Of Church Of St Ivo
entries.reason: The list entry dates the tomb chest to 1770.

sources.title: Tombchest of William Rattle, St Ive (list entry 1137084)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Tombchest. 1770. William Rattle of Cadson and retrains of wife and son. Ashlar slatestone.

entries.name: Maggoty Johnson's Grave
entries.reason: Samuel 'Maggoty' Johnson was buried here in 1773; the table tomb is dated 1773 (its brick plinth is 20th-century).

sources.title: Maggoty Johnson's Grave, Gawsworth (list entry 1329714)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Table tomb. Dated 1773. Stone slab on C20 brick plinth. Rectangular stone raised on brick base.

entries.name: Newark Cemetery
entries.reason: Newark Cemetery is the town's general cemetery (1856); it contains a war graves plot (Polish airmen of the Second World War) but is not itself a war cemetery, so 1856 is not a war-cemetery date.

entries.name: Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial
entries.reason: Americans who died around London during the First World War were buried in a plot at Brookwood; the permanent American cemetery was formed there in 1922.

sources.title: Brookwood American Cemetery and Memorial
sources.quote: After the Armistice in 1918, the dead from various temporary sites throughout England, Scotland and Ireland were brought to it.

sources.title: Brookwood American Cemetery
sources.author: Interment.net
sources.quote: Near London, a temporary plot in Brookwood Cemetery was allocated for Americans who died in and around the English capital.

entries.name: Cannock Chase German Military Cemetery
entries.reason: Wikidata's 1956 has no support: the Anglo-German agreement was made in 1959 and the cemetery was built 1959-67 and dedicated in June 1967.

sources.title: Cannock Chase German Military Cemetery
sources.quote: is maintained under the inter-government agreement by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission – was inaugurated and dedicated in June 1967

sources.title: Cannock Chase German Military Cemetery (list entry 1391922)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Cemetery building, memorial courtyard and adjoining terrace. 1959-67 by Harold Doffman of Doffman and Leach of Stafford

entries.name: Hull Paragon Interchange
entries.kind_label: Airport, bus station or tram depot
entries.reason: 1847 is the date of the railway station and hotel; the bus station and interchange that make this a bus station opened in September 2007.

sources.title: Hull Paragon Interchange
sources.quote: Hull Paragon Interchange opened on 16 September 2007, combining rail and bus station services on a single site.

entries.name: Blackpool Airport
entries.kind_label: Airport, bus station or tram depot
entries.reason: The site at Squires Gate was first used for aviation at the October 1909 flying meeting; it was a racecourse and hospital in 1911-24 and became a regular airport in the 1930s.

sources.title: Blackpool Airport
sources.quote: The airport site's first aviation use was in October 1909, when the UK's first official public Flying Meeting was held on a specially laid out site at Squires Gate

entries.name: Brighton City Airport
entries.kind_label: Airport, bus station or tram depot
entries.reason: The first flight from the Shoreham site was in 1910 and the aerodrome was officially opened in 1911.

sources.title: Brighton City Airport
sources.quote: The first flight from the site took place in 1910 and the airport officially opened in 1911.

entries.name: Bristol Filton Airport
entries.kind_label: Airport, bus station or tram depot
entries.reason: A small flying ground was set up at Filton in 1911; the airfield proper was laid out by the Royal Flying Corps in 1915 at the bottom of Filton Hill.

sources.title: Bristol Filton Airport
sources.quote: A small 'flying ground' was set up opposite Fairlawn Avenue in 1911, at the top of Filton Hill.

entries.name: Chichester/Goodwood Airport
entries.kind_label: Airport, bus station or tram depot
entries.reason: Wikidata's 1918 has no support: the airfield was built in the Second World War as RAF Westhampnett, a relief landing ground for Tangmere, and was in use by the Battle of Britain (1940).

sources.title: Chichester/Goodwood Airport
sources.quote: The airfield was built during the Second World War by the Royal Air Force as a relief landing ground for nearby RAF Tangmere.

entries.name: Workington bus station
entries.kind_label: Airport, bus station or tram depot
entries.reason: Opened by Cumberland Motor Services in March 1926 as the first purpose-built covered bus station in Great Britain.

sources.title: Workington bus station
sources.quote: It was opened on 19 March 1926 by Cumberland Motor Services as the first purpose-built covered bus station in Great Britain.

entries.name: Haymarket bus station
entries.kind_label: Airport, bus station or tram depot
entries.reason: The original bus station opened in 1930; it has been rebuilt twice, the second time on a slightly different site.

sources.title: Haymarket bus station, Newcastle upon Tyne
sources.quote: The original bus station opened in 1930 and was rebuilt in 1971.

entries.name: Victoria Coach Station
entries.kind_label: Airport, bus station or tram depot
entries.reason: Built 1931-32 by Wallis, Gilbert & Partners and opened in March 1932.

sources.title: Victoria Coach Station
sources.quote: Victoria Coach Station was commissioned by London Coastal Coaches, a consortium of coach operators, and opened on 10 March 1932 by Minister of Transport John Pybus.

entries.name: River lock and retaining walls to River Aire
entries.reason: Lock No. 1 of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal was built 1770-76 and the Leeds to Gargrave stretch opened here in 1777.

sources.title: River Lock and retaining walls to River Aire, Leeds (list entry 1255707)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Lock and retaining walls. 1770-1776. For the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Company.

entries.name: Wilts & Berks Canal
entries.reason: The canal was authorised in 1795 and completed and opened in 1810.

sources.title: Wilts and Berks Canal
sources.quote: The 52-mile (84 km) canal was opened in 1810, but abandoned in 1914 – a fate hastened by a breach at Stanley aqueduct in 1901.

entries.name: Macclesfield Canal
entries.reason: 1826 is the Act of Parliament and the start of construction (December 1826); the canal opened in 1831.

sources.title: Macclesfield Canal
sources.quote: The canal opened in 1831 and is 26.1 miles (42.0 km) long.

entries.name: Forth and Cart Canal
entries.reason: 1836 is the Act of Parliament; the canal was completed in 1840.

sources.title: Forth and Cart Canal
sources.quote: The Forth and Cart canal was authorised by an act of Parliament, the Forth and Cart Junction Canal Act 1836 (6 & 7 Will. 4. c. li), in May 1836 and was completed in 1840.

entries.name: Electricity Sub-Station
entries.kind_label: Power station, substation or telephone exchange
entries.age_text: built c. 1833 as a hearse house
entries.reason: The building was put up c. 1833 as the parish hearse house and only later became an electricity sub-station, so 1833 is not a date for a substation.

sources.title: Electricity Sub-Station, Church Street, Runcorn (list entry 1130437)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Hearse-house now sub-station circa 1833. Red sandstone with later blue quarry tile roof.

entries.name: Bloom Street Power Station
entries.kind_label: Power station, substation or telephone exchange
entries.reason: Manchester Corporation's Bloom Street (Winser Street) generating station opened in 1901. The listed building is also a separate Wikidata item (Q26546636), so this record may be a duplicate.

sources.title: Former Electricity Power Station, Winser Street, Manchester (list entry 1255031)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Electicity power generating station, now part electicity sub-station and part central-heating generator for the locality. 1901, altered.

sources.title: Bloom Street power station
sources.author: manchesterhistory.net
sources.quote: The station started to produce electricty for the city and nearby suburbs in 1901.

entries.name: Council Depot
entries.kind_label: Power station, substation or telephone exchange
entries.reason: Built in 1903 as an electricity generating station (by Mitchell and Sumner), later a council depot.

sources.title: Council Depot, White Hart Road, Plumstead (list entry 1271530)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Former electricity generating station, subsequently council depot. 1903 by Mitchell and Sumner.

entries.name: Q132496654
entries.kind_label: Power station, substation or telephone exchange
entries.reason: Telephone House, Carr Lane, Hull (central exchange and head office of the Hull telephone undertaking) was begun in 1961 and opened in 1964.

sources.title: Our history
sources.author: KCOM
sources.quote: Celebrating our Diamond Jubilee with the official opening of the new Central exchange and Head Office, Telephone House in Carr Lane Hull.

sources.title: History of the Hull telephone service
sources.author: britishtelephones.com
sources.quote: 1961 With an ever growing business, the company began the building of Telephone House.

entries.name: Foyers Power Station
entries.kind_label: Power station, substation or telephone exchange
entries.reason: 1969 is the start of work on the pumped-storage scheme, commissioned in 1974 (the earlier Foyers aluminium-works hydro station of 1896 is a different thing).

sources.title: Glendoe Hydro Scheme
sources.quote: Subsequently, Cruachan was commissioned in 1968, and Foyers in 1974, but both of these were pumped storage schemes.

entries.name: Braes of Doune Wind Farm
entries.kind_label: Power station, substation or telephone exchange
entries.reason: Wikidata's 2006 is the start of building; the wind farm was built and opened in 2007.

sources.title: Braes of Doune Wind Farm
sources.quote: Braes of Doune Wind Farm is a wind farm located close to Stirling, Scotland and opened in 2007.

entries.name: Glendoe Hydro Scheme
entries.kind_label: Power station, substation or telephone exchange
entries.reason: 2006 is the start of construction; the station generated from January 2009 and was opened in June 2009.

sources.title: Glendoe Hydro Scheme
sources.quote: Construction started in 2006, and Hochtief completed the scheme in 2009.

entries.name: Whitelee Wind Farm
entries.kind_label: Power station, substation or telephone exchange
entries.reason: 2006 is the start of construction; the first phase supplied the grid from January 2008 and the farm was officially opened in May 2009.

sources.title: Whitelee Wind Farm
sources.quote: However, Whitelee was generating power more than a year before this with the first phase of the wind farm supplying power to the electricity grid in January 2008.

entries.name: Dublin–Rosslare railway line
entries.kind_label: Railway line, signal box or funicular
entries.reason: The Westland Row to Kingstown section (the Dublin and Kingstown Railway), Ireland's first railway, opened in 1834; the rest of the line is later.

sources.title: Dublin–Rosslare railway line
sources.quote: is the oldest railway line in Ireland, and the first commuter railway in the world, opening in 1834.

entries.name: Esk Valley Line
entries.kind_label: Railway line, signal box or funicular
entries.reason: The Whitby to Grosmont section (Whitby and Pickering Railway) opened in 1835; the other parts of the line are later.

sources.title: Esk Valley line
sources.quote: The first section of line between Whitby Town and Grosmont opened in 1835, with an extension to Pickering opening on 26 May 1836.

entries.name: Derwent Valley Line
entries.kind_label: Railway line, signal box or funicular
entries.reason: The Derby to Ambergate section, built by the North Midland Railway, opened in 1839; Ambergate to Matlock followed in 1849.

sources.title: Derwent Valley line
sources.quote: The section from Derby to Ambergate was built by the North Midland Railway (which ran between Derby and Leeds) and was opened in 1839.

entries.name: Severn Beach line
entries.kind_label: Railway line, signal box or funicular
entries.reason: Wikidata's 1840 has no support; the first sections opened in 1865 as the Bristol Port Railway and Pier.

sources.title: Severn Beach line
sources.quote: The first sections of the line were opened in 1865 as part of the Bristol Port Railway and Pier; the section through Bristol was opened in 1875 as the Clifton Extension Railway.

entries.name: South Eastern main line
entries.kind_label: Railway line, signal box or funicular
entries.reason: The South Eastern Railway's line from London Bridge (via Redhill) to Tonbridge opened in May 1842.

sources.title: South Eastern Main Line
sources.quote: The line from London Bridge to Tunbridge opened on 26 May 1842.

entries.name: Padarn Railway
entries.kind_label: Railway line, signal box or funicular
entries.reason: The Padarn Railway opened in March 1843, replacing the earlier Dinorwic Railway (1824).

sources.title: Padarn Railway
sources.quote: The line opened on 3 March 1843, replacing the Dinorwic Railway.

entries.name: Wherry Lines
entries.kind_label: Railway line, signal box or funicular
entries.reason: Norwich to Great Yarmouth via Reedham opened in 1844 (Yarmouth and Norwich Railway).

sources.title: Wherry Lines
sources.quote: The route was opened from Norwich to Great Yarmouth by the Yarmouth and Norwich Railway in 1844, running via Reedham.

entries.name: Nottingham to Lincoln Line
entries.kind_label: Railway line, signal box or funicular
entries.reason: The line opened on 4 August 1846.

sources.title: Nottingham–Lincoln line
sources.quote: The line was inspected by General Pasley on 31 July 1846 and opened on 4 August 1846.

entries.name: Gartmorn Dam
entries.reason: Reservoir and dam built 1711-12 by George Sorocold to power pumps for the Alloa mines; the dam was rebuilt in stone in 1785.

sources.title: Gartmorn Dam
sources.quote: The dam, lake and associated waterworks were designed by and built, from 1711 to 1712, by English civil engineer George Sorocold.

entries.name: Dam On River Coquet 350 Metres Upstream Of Guyzance Bridge
entries.reason: Horseshoe dam built by John Smeaton in 1775, repaired in 1926.

sources.title: Dam on River Coquet 350 metres upstream of Guyzance Bridge (list entry 1153600)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Dam. 1775 by Smeaton for John Archbold of Acton and Edward Cook of Brainshaugh, repaired and cement skirt constructed 1926.

entries.name: Kilmannan Reservoir
entries.reason: The Forth and Clyde Canal Company built Kilmannan reservoir in 1776 to make good the water it had taken from the Glasgow bakers' mills on the Kelvin.

sources.title: Banton Loch
sources.quote: In response, in 1776, the canal company erected a reservoir at Kilmannan, about 25 kilometres (16 mi) to the west of Townhead

entries.name: Combs Reservoir
entries.reason: Built in 1797 as the first feeder reservoir of the Peak Forest Canal; the dam was raised 1834-40.

sources.title: Combs Reservoir
sources.quote: Combs was built in 1797 as the first reservoir to feed the Peak Forest Canal (which opened in 1800) at Whaley Bridge.

entries.name: Weir on River Goyt
entries.reason: The list entry dates the weir to c. 1805.

sources.title: Weir on River Goyt, Brabyns Park, Marple Bridge (list entry 1241826)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Weir. c.1805. Ashlar and roughly dressed stone. The segmental weir in flanked on either side by piers/retaining walls

entries.name: Drinking fountain and clock tower at Queen Mary College
entries.reason: A drinking fountain and clock tower is not a reservoir, dam, weir or waterworks; the list entry's 1840 also cannot be right, since it was given to the People's Palace (opened 1887) in memory of Baron de Stern.

entries.name: Mugdock Reservoir
entries.reason: 1856 falls during construction of the Loch Katrine scheme (begun 1855); the scheme, ending at Mugdock Reservoir, was opened in 1859 and the reservoir was in full use by 1860.

sources.title: Milngavie water treatment works
sources.quote: Part of the Victorian Loch Katrine water project, construction was started in 1855 and the works was opened by Queen Victoria in 1859

sources.title: Barrachan, Mugdock Reservoir (listed building)
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: Mugdock reservoir was opened in 1860 as part of the first phase of the Glasgow Corporation Water Works that brought water down from Loch Katrine.

entries.name: Samuel Gurney Drinking Fountain
entries.reason: A street drinking fountain is not a reservoir, dam, weir or waterworks.

entries.name: Plague Cross
entries.reason: This is a cross base with a later milestone inscription; 1604 is the plague of local tradition, not a date for the stone as a road marker, and the milestone inscription is undated.

sources.title: Plague Cross, Alne (list entry 1151296)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Traditionally connected with the plague of 1604 when it is said to have been a place of barter outside the village

entries.name: Milestone Opposite Gang Cottage
entries.reason: One of a series of milestones from St Germans to Launceston put up c. 1700 under the 1697 Act.

sources.title: Gang Milestone opposite Gang Cottage, St Ive (list entry 1392532)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: HISTORY: The milestone was erected circa 1700. It is one of a series that can be found, marking the route from St Germans to Launceston.

entries.name: The White Stone And Fragment Of Base Immediately To The East
entries.reason: The inscribed stone is said to be dated 1700; the inscription is damaged but its lettering looks at least that old.

sources.title: The White Stone and fragment of base, Withington (list entry 1180080)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Said to be dated 1700 but hard to date as inscription is damaged, nevertheless the lettering does appear at least that old.

entries.name: Old Cross
entries.age_text: medieval cross, a guide post from 1702
entries.reason: A medieval cross base reused as a guide post after guide posts were ordered at crossways in 1702 (inscription restored 1932); 1702 is its date as a road marker.

sources.title: Old Cross, St Lawrence Road, North Wingfield (list entry 1108907)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: The words cut upon it show/ that it was utilised as a guide post after such were/ ordered to be set up at crossways in the year 1702./

entries.name: Guide Post 100 Metres South Of Sycamore Farm
entries.reason: The guide post is inscribed 1705 on all four sides.

sources.title: Guide post 100 m south of Sycamore Farm, Hopton (list entry 1112545)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Milestone. Dated 1705. Gritstone pillar approximately 3 feet high, slightly damaged at the top.

entries.name: Old Milestone About 650 Yards South East From Red Cross
entries.reason: Inscription illegible; the list entry suggests it dates from the rebuilding of Wort's Causeway under William Wort's bequest (he died 1709). A weak date.

sources.title: Old Milestone about 650 yards south-east from Red Cross, Wort's Causeway (list entry 1331933)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Roadway originally Roman, but rebuilt at bequest of William Wort (died 1709), so the stone may date from then.

entries.name: Guide Stone Opposite Eagle Lodge Gates
entries.reason: The guide stone is inscribed with the date 1712.

sources.title: Guide Stone opposite Eagle Lodge Gates, Thornton Steward (list entry 1318578)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Guide stone. Dated 1712. Sandstone. 5-sided stone approximately one metre high.

entries.name: Milestone Approximately 15 Metres To North West Of Milehouse Farm
entries.reason: The milestone is inscribed 'Richmond 1712'.

sources.title: Milestone approximately 15 metres north-west of Milehouse Farm, Firby (list entry 1314989)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Milestone. Dated 1712. Limestone. Square-section pillar approximately 1 metre high set on a plinth.

entries.name: 36 Church Street
entries.reason: The c. 1840 classical building had its ground floor altered later for a bank (Barclays), so 1840 is the date of the building, not of a bank.

sources.title: No 36 Church Street (Barclay's Bank), Blackburn (list entry 1239364)
sources.author: Historic England

entries.name: York County Savings Bank
entries.reason: Built in 1841 to Anthony Salvin's design as the York County Savings Bank.
